claim: Lack of early infection-exposure has been associated with increased allergy-related disease (ARD) susceptibility.
source: Lack of early infection-exposure has been associated with increased allergy-related disease (ARD) susceptibility later in life, the so-called 'hygiene hypothesis' (Strachan, 1989; Bloomfield et al., 2006; Schaub et al., 2006) or 'old friends hypothesis' (Rook, 2010; Rook, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research (Strachan, 1989; Bloomfield et al., 2006; Schaub et al., 2006; Rook, 2010; Rook, 2011).

claim: Studies in high-income countries have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy for hepatitis A virus.
source: Studies, mainly in high-income countries (HICs), have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy, specifically for hepatitis A virus (Strachan, 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Strachan, 2000.

claim: Studies in high-income countries have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy for gut flora.
source: Studies, mainly in high-income countries (HICs), have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy, specifically for hepatitis A virus (Strachan, 2000), gut flora (Björkstén et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Björkstén et al., 1999.

claim: Studies in high-income countries have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy for intestinal parasites.
source: Studies, mainly in high-income countries (HICs), have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy, specifically for hepatitis A virus (Strachan, 2000), gut flora (Björkstén et al., 1999), intestinal parasites (Yazdanbakhsh and Matricardi, 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yazdanbakhsh and Matricardi, 2004.

claim: Studies in high-income countries have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy for mycobacteria.
source: Studies, mainly in high-income countries (HICs), have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy, specifically for hepatitis A virus (Strachan, 2000), gut flora (Björkstén et al., 1999), intestinal parasites (Yazdanbakhsh and Matricardi, 2004), mycobacteria (Shirakawa et al., 1997)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shirakawa et al., 1997.

claim: Studies in high-income countries have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy for malaria.
source: Studies, mainly in high-income countries (HICs), have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy, specifically for hepatitis A virus (Strachan, 2000), gut flora (Björkstén et al., 1999), intestinal parasites (Yazdanbakhsh and Matricardi, 2004), mycobacteria (Shirakawa et al., 1997), malaria (Lell et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lell et al., 2001.

claim: Studies in high-income countries have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy for total burden of infections.
source: Studies, mainly in high-income countries (HICs), have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy, specifically for hepatitis A virus (Strachan, 2000), gut flora (Björkstén et al., 1999), intestinal parasites (Yazdanbakhsh and Matricardi, 2004), mycobacteria (Shirakawa et al., 1997), malaria (Lell et al., 2001), total burden of infections (Martinez and Holt, 1999; Illi et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martinez and Holt, 1999; Illi et al., 2001.

claim: Studies in high-income countries have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy for farm animal sheds.
source: Studies, mainly in high-income countries (HICs), have highlighted the inverse relationship between pathogen-exposure and atopy, specifically for hepatitis A virus (Strachan, 2000), gut flora (Björkstén et al., 1999), intestinal parasites (Yazdanbakhsh and Matricardi, 2004), mycobacteria (Shirakawa et al., 1997), malaria (Lell et al., 2001), total burden of infections (Martinez and Holt, 1999; Illi et al., 2001), and farm animal sheds (Loss et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Loss et al., 2016.

claim: Some studies suggest no association between pathogen-exposure and atopy.
source: Despite increasing evidence indicating inverse relationships between pathogen-exposure and atopy, other studies suggest no association (Jarvis et al., 2004; Cooper et al., 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jarvis et al., 2004; Cooper et al., 2003.

claim: Some studies suggest increased risk of atopy following a combination of early infections.
source: Despite increasing evidence indicating inverse relationships between pathogen-exposure and atopy, other studies suggest no association (Jarvis et al., 2004; Cooper et al., 2003) or even increased risk of atopy following a combination of early infections (Seaton and Devereux, 2000; Bager et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Seaton and Devereux, 2000; Bager et al., 2002.

claim: It remains unclear which infections, and at which times, possibly contribute to reducing the risk of atopy or ARDs.
source: Therefore, it remains unclear which infections, and at which times, possibly contribute to reducing the risk of atopy or ARDs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the conflicting evidence presented in the literature review.

claim: There is a paucity of data from countries in tropical Africa where the infectious diseases burden remains high.
source: There is a paucity of data from countries in tropical Africa where the infectious diseases burden remains high, yet prevalence of ARDs remains low, despite reasonably high prevalence of atopy.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the existing literature.

claim: In tropical Africa, prevalence of ARDs remains low, despite reasonably high prevalence of atopy.
source: There is a paucity of data from countries in tropical Africa where the infectious diseases burden remains high, yet prevalence of ARDs remains low, despite reasonably high prevalence of atopy.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the epidemiological context.

claim: ARDs (eczema, wheeze, and rhinitis) decline with age, despite increasing atopy.
source: Similar to findings from HICs (Bach, 2002), we have shown previously that ARDs (eczema, wheeze, and rhinitis) decline with age, despite increasing atopy (Lule et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bach, 2002 and Lule et al., 2017.

source: In this Ugandan birth cohort, early childhood infection-exposure, notably to malaria, helminths, LRTI, and diarrhoea, is associated with lower prevalence of atopy and ARDs in later childhood.
evidence: The claim is supported by the overall findings from the latent class analysis and outcome associations.

claim: The Entebbe Mother and Baby Study (EMaBS) was based at Entebbe General Hospital, Uganda.
source: The EMaBS has been described previously (Elliott et al., 2007). Briefly, the EMaBS, based at Entebbe General Hospital, Uganda, originated as a trial of anthelminthic treatment in pregnancy and early childhood, in a 2 × 2 (×2) factorial design.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Elliott et al., 2007 and describes the study location.

claim: Eczema was defined as recurrent itchy rash with typical flexural distribution.

claim: SPT reactivity was assessed to Dermatophagoides mix (D. farinae and D. pteronyssinus), Blomia tropicalis, German cockroach, cat, mould, grass pollen, Bermuda grass, and peanut.
source: SPT reactivity to Dermatophagoides mix (D. farinae and D. pteronyssinus), Blomia tropicalis, German cockroach, cat, mould, grass pollen, Bermuda grass, and peanut (ALK-Abelló, Laboratory Specialities (Pty) Ltd, Randburg, South Africa) was assessed using standard methods (Heinzerling et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the allergens tested, supported by a citation to Heinzerling et al., 2013.

claim: A SPT test was classified as positive if there was a papule of average size >3 mm, in the presence of saline (negative) and histamine (positive) controls.
source: A test was classified as positive if there was a papule of average size >3 mm, in the presence of saline (negative) and histamine (positive) controls.
evidence: The claim describes the criteria for a positive test.

claim: Plasma IgE to house dust mite (D. pteronyssinus) and German cockroach (Blatella germanica) was measured using an in-house ELISA.
source: Plasma IgE to the commonest allergens in this setting (house dust mite [D. pteronyssinus] and German cockroach [Blatella germanica]) (Mpairwe et al., 2008) was measured using an in-house ELISA as previously described (Mpairwe et al., 2011; Nkurunungi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim describes the method used, supported by citations to Mpairwe et al., 2008, 2011 and Nkurunungi et al., 2018.

claim: The in-house ELISA assay was optimised to work with 20-fold diluted samples, with a lower detection limit of 15.625 ng/ml (equivalent to 312.5 ng/ml in undiluted plasma).
source: Because of the dynamic range of our in-house assay, it was not possible to use undiluted plasma, hence we optimised our assay to work with 20-fold diluted samples, with a lower detection limit of 15.625 ng/ml (equivalent to 312.5 ng/ml in undiluted plasma).
evidence: The claim describes the technical specifications of the assay.

claim: Results from the in-house ELISA were positively correlated with those from ImmunoCAP for both dust mite and cockroach.
source: We have previously shown that results from our ELISA were positively correlated with those from ImmunoCAP for both dust mite and cockroach (Sanya et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sanya et al., 2019.

claim: Latent class analysis (LCA) was used to classify participants into latent classes based on infection-exposure during the first 5 years of life.
source: Since infection experience is an unobservable construct which can be inferred from multiple observed infections, we used the LC analysis (LCA) framework which has been shown to flexibly divide a population into mutually exclusive subgroups (Goodman, 1974; Lanza et al., 2007; Nylund-Gibson and Choi, 2018; Velicer et al., 1996; Ryoo et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim describes the statistical method used, supported by multiple citations.

claim: LCA models were fitted, successively increasing the number of classes up to a seven-class solution.
source: We fitted LCA models using infection-exposure variables as indicators. Models were fitted, successively increasing the number of classes up to a seven-class solution.
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: Two models were fitted: one considering infection-exposure during the first year of life (infancy) and the other using cumulative infection experience over the first 5 years.
source: Two models were fitted: one considering infection-exposure during the first year of life (infancy) and the other using cumulative infection experience over the first 5 years, with no a priori restrictions to find consistent classes across the two models.
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: The Bayesian information criterion (BIC), adjusted BIC (ABIC), consistent Akaike information criterion (CAIC), and entropy were used to guide the choice of optimal number of classes.
source: We used the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), adjusted BIC (ABIC), consistent Akaike information criterion (CAIC), and entropy to guide the choice of optimal number of classes (Lanza et al., 2007; Swanson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim describes the statistical criteria used, supported by citations to Lanza et al., 2007 and Swanson et al., 2012.

claim: Multiple-group LCA was conducted to establish whether measurement invariance across sex holds.
source: We conducted multiple-group LCA (Lanza et al., 2007) to establish whether measurement invariance across sex holds.
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach used, supported by a citation to Lanza et al., 2007.

claim: Covariates (maternal area of residence, maternal history of asthma or eczema, and maternal and household socio-economic status at enrolment) were incorporated to establish whether these impacted the probability of class membership.
source: We incorporated the covariates maternal area of residence, maternal history of asthma or eczema, and maternal and household socio-economic status (SES) at enrolment, to establish whether these impacted the probability of class membership, through multinomial logistic regression (Lanza et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim describes the analytical approach used, supported by a citation to Lanza et al., 2007.

claim: Maternal SES was determined by level of education, personal income, and occupation.
source: Maternal SES was determined by level of education, personal income, and occupation while household SES was based on building materials and the number of rooms and items owned (Muhangi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim describes how SES was measured, supported by a citation to Muhangi et al., 2007.

claim: Household SES was based on building materials and the number of rooms and items owned.

evidence: The claim describes how SES was measured, supported by a citation to Muhangi et al., 2007.

claim: All models were estimated using SAS version 9.4 via PROC LCA which handles missing data on LC indicators under the missing at random assumption.
source: All models were estimated using SAS version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC) via PROC LCA which handles missing data on LC indicators under the missing at random assumption (Lanza et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim describes the software and method used, supported by a citation to Lanza et al., 2007.

claim: In this tropical African birth cohort children can be classified into two LCs based on their early childhood infection experience.
source: In conclusion, we show that in this tropical African birth cohort children can be classified into two LCs based on their early childhood infection experience and that exposure to common infections, mainly malaria, during the first year of life, was associated with lower proportions of ARDs in later childhood.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's findings from the latent class analysis.

claim: With cumulative infection experience over all the first 5 years, exposure to infections, mainly helminths, was associated with lower probabilities of SPT positivity in later childhood.

claim: Infancy is a critical period during which the risk of ARDs in later childhood is established.
source: LCA for first-year infection-exposure demonstrated the strong inverse association between infectious illnesses in infancy and ARDs in later childhood. On the other hand, LCA for cumulative infection experience over the first 5 years only illustrated strong inverse associations with atopy (SPT positivity). This suggests that infancy is a critical period during which the risk of ARDs in later childhood is established.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of first-year and 5-year cumulative infection analyses.

claim: Measurement invariance by sex holds for the latent class models.
source: Multiple-group LCA showed that measurement invariance by sex holds, based on the likelihood ratio difference test (p-value = 0.379 and p-value = 0.558 at year 1 and year 5, respectively) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the results of the multiple-group LCA test.
